claim: WTAP was clustered and formed condensate-like patterns in cells during RNA virus (VSV) infection.
source: we infected cells with RNA virus Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV) or DNA virus Herpes Simplex Virus-1 (HSV-1), and conducted the immunofluorescence experiments. Surprisingly, we found WTAP was clustered and formed condensate-like patterns in cells during virus infection (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which are experimental observations.

claim: WTAP was clustered and formed condensate-like patterns in cells during DNA virus (HSV-1) infection.
source: we infected cells with RNA virus Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV) or DNA virus Herpes Simplex Virus-1 (HSV-1), and conducted the immunofluorescence experiments. Surprisingly, we found WTAP was clustered and formed condensate-like patterns in cells during virus infection (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which are experimental observations.

claim: IFN-β stimulation increased the number of WTAP condensate formation.
source: We then stimulated cells with IFN-β and observed the increasing number of WTAP condensate formation (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating increased WTAP condensates after IFN-β stimulation.

claim: METTL3 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) during m6A modification process.
source: Previous studies have reported that some components in the methyltransferase complex, such as METTL3 or YTHDFs, undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) during m6A modification process (Han et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Han et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022a).

claim: YTHDFs undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) during m6A modification process.
source: Previous studies have reported that some components in the methyltransferase complex, such as METTL3 or YTHDFs, undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) during m6A modification process (Han et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Han et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022a).

claim: WTAP IDR was predicted to span amino acids from 245 to 396.
source: By searching WTAP protein structure (within part of MTC complex) in protein structure bank (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/7VF2), we found that WTAP IDR was predicted to span amino acids from 245 to 396, giving a clue that WTAP might have the ability to undergo phase separation (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of WTAP protein structure from a protein structure database, which is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Recombinant mCherry-WTAP automatically formed liquid-like condensates in vitro.
source: Observation under microscope showed that mCherry-WTAP automatically formed liquid-like condensates which could be reversed by 1,6-hexanediol (hex), an inhibitor of phase separation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct microscopic observation of recombinant protein behavior in vitro, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol (hex) is an inhibitor of phase separation.
source: Observation under microscope showed that mCherry-WTAP automatically formed liquid-like condensates which could be reversed by 1,6-hexanediol (hex), an inhibitor of phase separation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about the function of 1,6-hexanediol.

claim: WTAP condensates formed by mCherry-WTAP could be reversed by 1,6-hexanediol.
source: Observation under microscope showed that mCherry-WTAP automatically formed liquid-like condensates which could be reversed by 1,6-hexanediol (hex), an inhibitor of phase separation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating the effect of hex on WTAP condensates.

claim: Fusion of WTAP condensates were observed and larger condensates were formed in vitro.
source: Fusion of condensates were observed and larger condensates were formed in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: WTAP undergoes phase separation in vitro.
source: These data together confirmed that WTAP underwent phase separation in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: IFN-β stimulation increased the number of WTAP condensates in mCherry-WTAP-rescued HeLa cells.
source: A few WTAP condensates were discovered in untreated cells while an increasing number of WTAP condensates were observed under IFN-β stimulation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in cells expressing mCherry-WTAP.

claim: Hex treatment dissipated WTAP condensates in IFN-β treated cells into a dispersed pattern.
source: After hex treatment, WTAP condensates in IFN-β treated cells dissipated into a dispersed pattern (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Hex treatment in virus-infected cells disrupted the formation of WTAP condensates.
source: Similarly, hex treatment in virus-infected cells also disrupted the formation of WTAP condensates (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WTAP exhibited lower recovery intensity in untreated cells in FRAP experiments.
source: We next checked the mobility of WTAP condensates by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments. Intriguingly, WTAP exhibited lower recovery intensity in untreated cells but higher mobility with rapid recovery intensity in IFN-β-treated cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: WTAP exhibited higher mobility with rapid recovery intensity in IFN-β-treated cells in FRAP experiments.
source: We next checked the mobility of WTAP condensates by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments. Intriguingly, WTAP exhibited lower recovery intensity in untreated cells but higher mobility with rapid recovery intensity in IFN-β-treated cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: WTAP underwent gel-like phase separation under basal conditions.
source: These results suggested a potential dynamic transformation in WTAP phase separation. While WTAP underwent gel-like phase separation under basal conditions, IFN-β induced its phase transition to form the liquid-like condensates under physiological conditions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the FRAP data showing lower mobility in untreated cells.

claim: IFN-β induced WTAP phase transition to form liquid-like condensates under physiological conditions.
source: These results suggested a potential dynamic transformation in WTAP phase separation. While WTAP underwent gel-like phase separation under basal conditions, IFN-β induced its phase transition to form the liquid-like condensates under physiological conditions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the FRAP data showing higher mobility in IFN-β-treated cells.

claim: Serine (Ser), Glutamine (Gln), Glutamate (Glu), and Leucine (Leu) were present at significantly higher levels than other amino acids within WTAP.
source: We then analyzed the abundance of amino acids and found that Serine (Ser), Glutamine (Gln), Glutamate (Glu), and Leucine (Leu) were present at significantly higher levels than other amino acids within WTAP (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by amino acid composition analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Gln and Leu were mainly located in the N-terminal domain (NTD) of WTAP.
source: Gln and Leu were mainly located in the N-terminal domain (NTD) while Ser was mostly enriched in the C-terminal domain (CTD), implying the distinct properties of NTD and CTD (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by amino acid distribution analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ser was mostly enriched in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of WTAP.
source: Gln and Leu were mainly located in the N-terminal domain (NTD) while Ser was mostly enriched in the C-terminal domain (CTD), implying the distinct properties of NTD and CTD (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by amino acid distribution analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IDR of WTAP were predicted to cover the entire serine-rich CTD region.
source: Notably, IDR of WTAP were predicted to cover the entire serine-rich CTD region.
evidence: The claim is based on structural prediction analysis of WTAP.

claim: Hydrogen bond between serine side chain mediated the intermolecular interaction and LLPS of FUS.
source: Previous researches reported that hydrogen bond between serine side chain mediated the intermolecular interaction and LLPS of FUS.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge from previous research, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: Abnormal glutamine-repeat resulted in the formation of β-sheet and solid/gel-like aggregates with lower mobility.
source: In addition, abnormal glutamine-repeat resulted in the formation of β-sheet and solid/gel-like aggregates with lower mobility (Perutz, 1996; Tanaka et al., 2001), which were related to neurodegenerative diseases like Huntington's disease (Gourfinkel-An et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Perutz, 1996; Tanaka et al., 2001).

claim: Abnormal glutamine-repeat aggregates were related to neurodegenerative diseases like Huntington's disease.
source: In addition, abnormal glutamine-repeat resulted in the formation of β-sheet and solid/gel-like aggregates with lower mobility (Perutz, 1996; Tanaka et al., 2001), which were related to neurodegenerative diseases like Huntington's disease (Gourfinkel-An et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study (Gourfinkel-An et al., 1997).

claim: Full-length WTAP formed liquid condensates in vitro.
source: As predicted, we found full-length WTAP and CTD WTAP formed liquid condensates, while NTD of WTAP clustered and formed aggregates with lower mobility, which was confirmed through FRAP experiments (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: CTD WTAP formed liquid condensates in vitro.
source: As predicted, we found full-length WTAP and CTD WTAP formed liquid condensates, while NTD of WTAP clustered and formed aggregates with lower mobility, which was confirmed through FRAP experiments (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: NTD of WTAP clustered and formed aggregates with lower mobility in vitro.
source: As predicted, we found full-length WTAP and CTD WTAP formed liquid condensates, while NTD of WTAP clustered and formed aggregates with lower mobility, which was confirmed through FRAP experiments (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Full-length WTAP transited from liquid-like condensates to aggregates after incubation for several minutes in vitro.
source: Intriguingly, we further observed that full-length WTAP transited from liquid-like condensates to aggregates after incubation for several minutes while CTD of WTAP remained liquid phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: CTD of WTAP remained liquid phase after incubation for several minutes in vitro.
source: Intriguingly, we further observed that full-length WTAP transited from liquid-like condensates to aggregates after incubation for several minutes while CTD of WTAP remained liquid phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Phosphorylation level of WTAP was significantly decreased under IFN-β stimulation.
source: We first detected the phosphorylation level of WTAP through immunoprecipitation (IP) assay and found that phosphorylation of WTAP was significantly decreased under IFN-β stimulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by IP assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PPP4 presented the strongest interaction with WTAP among family of protein phosphatases (PPPs).
source: Through IP assays, we aimed to identify the phosphatases that dephosphorylate WTAP, thus checked the interaction between WTAP and family of protein phosphatases (PPPs), and found that PPP4 presented the strongest interaction with WTAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by IP assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IFN-β stimulation promoted the interaction between WTAP and PPP4.
source: IFN-β stimulation promoted the interaction between WTAP and PPP4 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IP assay data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of PPP4 significantly restrained the dephosphorylation of WTAP in IFN-β treated cells.
source: Both knockdown of PPP4 and the potent PPP4 inhibitor fostriecin treatment significantly restrained the dephosphorylation of WTAP in IFN-β treated cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IP assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fostriecin is a potent PPP4 inhibitor.
source: Both knockdown of PPP4 and the potent PPP4 inhibitor fostriecin treatment significantly restrained the dephosphorylation of WTAP in IFN-β treated cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about fostriecin.

claim: Fostriecin treatment significantly restrained the dephosphorylation of WTAP in IFN-β treated cells.
source: Both knockdown of PPP4 and the potent PPP4 inhibitor fostriecin treatment significantly restrained the dephosphorylation of WTAP in IFN-β treated cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IP assay data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IFN-β regulated dephosphorylation of WTAP through PPP4.
source: These data indicated that IFN-β regulated dephosphorylation of WTAP through PPP4.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data showing PPP4 interaction with WTAP and effects of PPP4 knockdown/inhibition.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified six phosphorylated serine/threonine sites within WTAP.
source: MS results identified six phosphorylated serine/threonine sites within WTAP, five of which were located in the CTD (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Five of the six phosphorylated serine/threonine sites within WTAP were located in the CTD.
source: MS results identified six phosphorylated serine/threonine sites within WTAP, five of which were located in the CTD (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Introducing three or more phosphorylation-mimic mutations in WTAP promoted protein aggregation in vitro.
source: We found that introducing three or more phosphorylation-mimic mutations in WTAP promoted protein aggregation (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The 5ST-D mutant of WTAP induced aggregation in vitro.
source: While the 5ST-D mutant induced aggregation, the 5ST-A mutant formed liquid condensates comparable to wild-type (WT) WTAP, which remained unphosphorylated in the E. coli expression system lacking endogenous kinase activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The 5ST-A mutant of WTAP formed liquid condensates comparable to wild-type (WT) WTAP in vitro.
source: While the 5ST-D mutant induced aggregation, the 5ST-A mutant formed liquid condensates comparable to wild-type (WT) WTAP, which remained unphosphorylated in the E. coli expression system lacking endogenous kinase activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: E. coli expression system lacks endogenous kinase activity.
source: While the 5ST-D mutant induced aggregation, the 5ST-A mutant formed liquid condensates comparable to wild-type (WT) WTAP, which remained unphosphorylated in the E. coli expression system lacking endogenous kinase activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about E. coli expression systems.

claim: Mobility of WT WTAP was significantly higher than that of its 5ST-D mutant in vitro in FRAP experiments.
source: We next conducted FRAP experiments and found that mobility of WT WTAP as well as 5ST-A mutant was significantly higher than that of its 5ST-D mutant in vitro (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mobility of 5ST-A mutant was significantly higher than that of 5ST-D mutant in vitro in FRAP experiments.
source: We next conducted FRAP experiments and found that mobility of WT WTAP as well as 5ST-A mutant was significantly higher than that of its 5ST-D mutant in vitro (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Hyperphosphorylated WT WTAP in untreated cells showed lower mobility as 5ST-D mutant compared to phosphorylation-deficient 5ST-A mutant.
source: However, hyperphosphorylated WT WTAP in untreated cells showed lower mobility as 5ST-D mutant compared to phosphorylation-deficient 5ST-A mutant, while IFN-β-induced dephosphorylation promoted the recovery efficiency of WT WTAP as higher as 5ST-A mutants of WTAP (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data in cells shown in Figure 2H.

claim: IFN-β-induced dephosphorylation promoted the recovery efficiency of WT WTAP as high as 5ST-A mutants of WTAP.
source: However, hyperphosphorylated WT WTAP in untreated cells showed lower mobility as 5ST-D mutant compared to phosphorylation-deficient 5ST-A mutant, while IFN-β-induced dephosphorylation promoted the recovery efficiency of WT WTAP as higher as 5ST-A mutants of WTAP (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data in cells shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The liquid condensates of WTAP after IFN-β stimulation was blunted in PPP4 knocked-down cells.
source: Additionally, we found the liquid condensates of WTAP after IFN-β stimulation was blunted in PPP4 knocked-down cells and fostriecin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H), revealed that IFN-β triggered PPP4-mediated dephosphorylation of WTAP controlled the phase transition of WTAP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: The liquid condensates of WTAP after IFN-β stimulation was blunted by fostriecin treatment.
source: Additionally, we found the liquid condensates of WTAP after IFN-β stimulation was blunted in PPP4 knocked-down cells and fostriecin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H), revealed that IFN-β triggered PPP4-mediated dephosphorylation of WTAP controlled the phase transition of WTAP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: IFN-β triggered PPP4-mediated dephosphorylation of WTAP controlled the phase transition of WTAP.
source: Additionally, we found the liquid condensates of WTAP after IFN-β stimulation was blunted in PPP4 knocked-down cells and fostriecin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H), revealed that IFN-β triggered PPP4-mediated dephosphorylation of WTAP controlled the phase transition of WTAP.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data showing effects of PPP4 knockdown and inhibition on WTAP phase separation.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of WTAP tended to form aggregates with low mobility due to electrostatically repulsed between phosphorylated serine sites.
source: Taken together, we validated hyperphosphorylation of WTAP tended to form aggregates with low mobility due to electrostatically repulsed between phosphorylated serine sites, while hypophosphorylation of WTAP promoted the mobility and forms liquid condensates.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental data and known principles of electrostatic repulsion.

claim: Hypophosphorylation of WTAP promoted the mobility and forms liquid condensates.
source: Taken together, we validated hyperphosphorylation of WTAP tended to form aggregates with low mobility due to electrostatically repulsed between phosphorylated serine sites, while hypophosphorylation of WTAP promoted the mobility and forms liquid condensates.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data comparing phosphorylation mutants.

claim: IFN-β-mediated dephosphorylation promotes the transition from aggregates to liquid-phase of WTAP both in vitro and in cells.
source: IFN-β-mediated dephosphorylation promotes the transition from aggregates to liquid-phase of WTAP both in vitro and in cells (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented throughout the section.

claim: m6A modification affected antiviral activity through ISG mRNAs stabilization.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (McFadden et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020b).

claim: 1440 genes were up-regulated in response to IFN-β stimulation for 6 hr in WTAPsgRNA THP-1 cells.
source: we generated WTAPsgRNA THP-1 cells using the CRISPR-Cas9 system, and performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) followed by bioinformatic analysis, and uncovered that 1440 and 1689 genes were up-regulated in response to IFN-β stimulation for 6 and 12 hr, respectively (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 1689 genes were up-regulated in response to IFN-β stimulation for 12 hr in WTAPsgRNA THP-1 cells.
source: we generated WTAPsgRNA THP-1 cells using the CRISPR-Cas9 system, and performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) followed by bioinformatic analysis, and uncovered that 1440 and 1689 genes were up-regulated in response to IFN-β stimulation for 6 and 12 hr, respectively (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 441 ISGs exhibited elevated expression in WTAPsgRNA cells, including IFIT1, IFIT2, OAS1, and OAS2.
source: Among this, 441 ISGs exhibited elevated expression in WTAPsgRNA cells, including IFIT1, IFIT2, OAS1, and OAS2, which were enriched in various immune-related pathways (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: 441 ISGs with elevated expression in WTAPsgRNA cells were enriched in various immune-related pathways.
source: Among this, 441 ISGs exhibited elevated expression in WTAPsgRNA cells, including IFIT1, IFIT2, OAS1, and OAS2, which were enriched in various immune-related pathways (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WTAP showed no effect on the expression level of transcription factor STAT1 under IFN-β stimulation.
source: We also found that WTAP showed no effect on both the expression level and the phosphorylation level of transcription factors STAT1, STAT2, and IRF9 under IFN-β stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that changes of WTAP-regulated changes in ISGs expression were independent of phosphorylation level of indicated transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: WTAP showed no effect on the phosphorylation level of transcription factor STAT1 under IFN-β stimulation.
source: We also found that WTAP showed no effect on both the expression level and the phosphorylation level of transcription factors STAT1, STAT2, and IRF9 under IFN-β stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that changes of WTAP-regulated changes in ISGs expression were independent of phosphorylation level of indicated transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: WTAP showed no effect on the expression level of transcription factor STAT2 under IFN-β stimulation.
source: We also found that WTAP showed no effect on both the expression level and the phosphorylation level of transcription factors STAT1, STAT2, and IRF9 under IFN-β stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that changes of WTAP-regulated changes in ISGs expression were independent of phosphorylation level of indicated transcription factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Changes of WTAP-regulated changes in ISGs expression were independent of phosphorylation level of STAT1, STAT2, and IRF9.

evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that WTAP does not affect transcription factor phosphorylation.

claim: The majority of WTAP-dependent m6A modification peaks were located in coding sequences (CDS).
source: Consensus m6A modified core motifs were enriched in our samples and the majority of WTAP-dependent m6A modification peaks were located in coding sequences (CDS) and 3'- untranslated regions (UTR) (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The majority of WTAP-dependent m6A modification peaks were located in 3'- untranslated regions (UTR).
source: Consensus m6A modified core motifs were enriched in our samples and the majority of WTAP-dependent m6A modification peaks were located in coding sequences (CDS) and 3'- untranslated regions (UTR) (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: A group of ISGs that was m6A modified in control cells showed diminished modification in WTAPsgRNA cells.
source: A group of ISGs that was m6A modified in control cells but showed diminished modification in WTAPsgRNA cells were clustered in the IFN-associated pathway through MeRIP-seq assays, verifying the WTAP-dependent m6A modification of ISG mRNAs during IFN-β stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: ISGs with diminished m6A modification in WTAPsgRNA cells were clustered in the IFN-associated pathway.
source: A group of ISGs that was m6A modified in control cells but showed diminished modification in WTAPsgRNA cells were clustered in the IFN-associated pathway through MeRIP-seq assays, verifying the WTAP-dependent m6A modification of ISG mRNAs during IFN-β stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Around 64.29% of core ISGs were m6A modified.
source: Notably, around 64.29% of core ISGs and 61.90% of WTAP down-regulated ISGs were m6A modified, which was consistent with the similar percentage in previous studies (McFadden et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2019; Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Around 61.90% of WTAP down-regulated ISGs were m6A modified.
source: Notably, around 64.29% of core ISGs and 61.90% of WTAP down-regulated ISGs were m6A modified, which was consistent with the similar percentage in previous studies (McFadden et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2019; Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The percentage of m6A modified ISGs was consistent with the similar percentage in previous studies.
source: Notably, around 64.29% of core ISGs and 61.90% of WTAP down-regulated ISGs were m6A modified, which was consistent with the similar percentage in previous studies (McFadden et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2019; Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies (McFadden et al., 2021; Winkler et al., 2019).

claim: The topology of ISGs m6A sites revealed a strong preference for CDS localization compared to global m6A deposition.
source: The topology of ISGs m6A sites was analyzed, revealing a strong preference for CDS localization compared to global m6A deposition (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by topology analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: MeRIP-qPCR assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on IFIT1 in WTAPsgRNA cells.
source: MeRIP-quantitative real-time-polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on WTAP-down-regulated ISGs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, OAS1, and OAS2 (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: MeRIP-qPCR assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on IFIT2 in WTAPsgRNA cells.
source: MeRIP-quantitative real-time-polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on WTAP-down-regulated ISGs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, OAS1, and OAS2 (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: MeRIP-qPCR assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on OAS1 in WTAPsgRNA cells.
source: MeRIP-quantitative real-time-polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on WTAP-down-regulated ISGs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, OAS1, and OAS2 (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: MeRIP-qPCR assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on OAS2 in WTAPsgRNA cells.
source: MeRIP-quantitative real-time-polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays confirmed the reduced m6A modification level on WTAP-down-regulated ISGs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, OAS1, and OAS2 (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: m6A deposition was reported to affect the decay of mRNA.
source: Given that m6A deposition was reported to affect various aspects of RNA, especially for the decay of mRNA (Oerum et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014), we also checked the mRNA stabilization by inhibiting synthesis of nascent mRNA using Actinomycin D (Act D), as well as the expression level of these ISGs by qPCR assay.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Oerum et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: WTAP deficiency stabilized ISG mRNAs.
source: Our results showed that WTAP deficiency stabilized ISG mRNAs, leading to their up-regulated expression (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA decay assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: WTAP deficiency led to up-regulated expression of ISGs.
source: Our results showed that WTAP deficiency stabilized ISG mRNAs, leading to their up-regulated expression (Figure 3J and K).

claim: Transcription factors SMAD2/3, STAT5B, KLF9, and CEBPZ are found to recruit MTC on transcriptional start sites (TSS).
source: Transcription factors SMAD2/3, STAT5B, KLF9, and CEBPZ are found to recruit MTC on transcriptional start sites (TSS) and specifically direct the m6A modification on a subset of downstream transcripts mRNA CDS region, thereby affecting the cell fate decision (Barbieri et al., 2017; Bertero et al., 2018; Bhattarai et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Barbieri et al., 2017; Bertero et al., 2018; Bhattarai et al., 2024).
